design_detail: Review article in the British Journal of Anaesthesia (advance access 28 July 2005; eight pages, 84 references) by a single author at a private hospital in Queensland, Australia (his specialty is not stated in the paper). The aim is to clarify interactions between monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and opioid analgesics using recent data on serotonin toxicity, its clinical features and each drug’s strength as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SRI) in laboratory assays. One sentence describes the search for opioid-related reports (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, about 40 reports, listed on the author’s website). Tables 1 to 3 are reproduced from the author’s own website document (reference 29). The treatment section gives doses, which this card does not record.
can_establish: How one author reads the old and recent literature on pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan, fentanyl and other opioids taken with MAOIs, in light of each drug’s strength as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor in laboratory assays and of which opioids have and have not been reported in cases, and what a 1968 hospital test of pethidine in 15 patients did and did not look for.
cannot_establish: How often any opioid taken with an MAOI causes serotonin toxicity or death (no rate is given, and the author says the basis for an accurate estimate is insufficient); whether the individual reports he counts were serotonin toxicity (he judges many by a subjective reading of old descriptions); whether opioids with no reports are safe, since absence of reports is the main evidence for them; or whether laboratory transporter binding predicts risk in people.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The case evidence is about 40 reports of serotonin toxicity with opioid analgesics found by a search of the listed papers and standard databases and listed on the author’s website, outside the paper; the paper cites a few by reference number. The Hunter Area Toxicology Service’s more than 2,000 overdose cases are cited for the diagnostic rules.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond the one-sentence description of the search (p. 437).
sample.selection_effects: Case reports mostly from the 1950s to the 1970s, written before serotonin toxicity was defined and re-read by the author by a subjective interpretation (p. 437); reports exist because something happened, so the many uneventful uses are unseen (the author says this of fentanyl); the transporter-binding figures come from several sources, species and methods that the author says cannot be compared directly (Table 2 caption).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Exposure is as reported in the cited case reports (not read individually); drug potency is in-vitro binding to the serotonin transporter (Ki in nanomolar; a lower value is a stronger reuptake inhibitor) from the sources cited in Table 2, mostly Codd and colleagues.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the causes. Study conditions only: in the 1968 test the author describes, graded injections of pethidine up to a maximum single dose of 75 mg and morphine up to 7.5 mg were given to 15 patients. Treatment doses are in the paper and are not recorded here.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The review concerns MAOIs (irreversible, non-selective, or the reversible moclobemide) taken with opioids, serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin releasers; the reports it counts often involved anaesthesia and other drugs, which the paper does not itemise.

comparison.controls: The review compares opioids by their strength as serotonin reuptake inhibitors in laboratory assays and by whether cases have been reported. The only controlled human data are the 1968 test of pethidine, morphine and water in 15 patients (p. 437).

outcomes.instruments: Serotonin toxicity as the author reads it from report descriptions, using the triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity, autonomic hyperactivity and altered mental status and the Hunter decision rules; serotonin transporter binding (Ki).
outcomes.validity_norms: The author states that binding affinities below 1 nM are invariably associated with the ability to precipitate toxicity with MAOIs and that 1 to 10 nM is borderline (p. 436); the phenylpiperidine opioids with values in Table 2 lie above that range (14.1 to 760 nM) and are called weak or borderline (p. 437), and morphine, codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone lie above 100,000 nM.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed. The reports with MAOIs column of Table 2 rates each drug as definite, possible, uncertain or none, with no stated criteria.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new analysis and no rates. Table 2 (p. 436), serotonin transporter binding in nM (lower is stronger) and reports with MAOIs: SSRIs 0.13 to 2.2, definite, frequent fatalities; clomipramine 0.14, definite, frequent fatalities; imipramine 1.3, definite, occasional fatalities; amitriptyline 4.3, none; venlafaxine 8, definite, fatalities; morphine 500,000 and over 100,000, none; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone over 100,000, none; tramadol 760 and 528, definite, possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413, definite, some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain (one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death reported); remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known but unlikely. The 1968 test (p. 437): 15 patients, none had serotonergic symptoms at a maximum single pethidine dose of 75 mg; reflexes and clonus were not examined. The Treatment section (p. 438) repeats that serotonin toxicity needing admission occurred in 15% of SSRI overdoses and that more than 50% of MAOI or reversible-MAOI plus SRI overdoses had severe toxicity (reference 38, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: The case list behind the table (about 40 reports) is on the author’s website and not in the paper, so the basis for each definite or possible cannot be checked from the paper. The abstract, the discussion of the phenylpiperidine opioids (p. 437) and the conclusion (p. 439) place methadone among opioids involved in or able to cause toxicity with MAOIs, while Table 2 says no reports are known for it; the Table 1 caption names fatalities only with pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and possibly fentanyl, while the abstract says pethidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and propoxyphene have all been involved in reactions with MAOIs including some fatalities.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A single author’s reading of the opioid literature: morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine have no reports and are not serotonin reuptake inhibitors; pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan are weak reuptake inhibitors with reports of serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, some fatal; fentanyl is uncertain (one case, one possible death); methadone is a weak reuptake inhibitor with no reports known. He judges the risk with known serotonergic opioids to be probably low but unpredictable, and says there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate for fentanyl.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says pethidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and propoxyphene “have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities)” and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine “do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs” (p. 434); the conclusion says the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low (p. 439). Gaps: (1) Table 2 says no reports are known for methadone and the Table 1 caption names fatalities with pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and possibly fentanyl, against the abstract’s all and some fatalities; (2) the statement for the morphine-type drugs rests on absence of reports and on binding assays, not on tests in people taking MAOIs; (3) the case list is on the author’s website, and old reports, written before serotonin toxicity was defined, are judged by a subjective interpretation; (4) the 1968 test, which found no toxicity and did not look for clonus or reflexes, is read as confirming the spectrum concept; (5) probably low has no denominator.

timeline.event: Evans-Prosser: graded injections of pethidine or morphine or water in 15 patients, none with serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus not examined (as described in this review; not read).

Codd and colleagues: serotonin and noradrenaline uptake inhibition by centrally acting analgesics, the only published screen of several opioids by one method (reference 10, as described in this review; not read).
Vuori and colleagues: four deaths with MDMA and moclobemide in Finland, cited in this review as a recent case series (the paper read for this library).

Buckley and colleagues cite this review among six reviews of case reports for the statement that nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI; they list pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan as opioids associated with toxicity (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: A single-author review whose opioid conclusions are repeated by Buckley and colleagues (2014), who cite it, so the two are not independent evidence. No newer review specific to opioids with MAOIs was read for this library, and the case reports and the 1968 test are known here only as this review describes them.

funding.declared_conflicts: None declared; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author at Pioneer Valley Private Hospital, Mackay, Queensland (p. 434). The acknowledgements thank his wife for maintaining the computers and programs used (p. 439). Tables 1 to 3 and the case list come from the author’s own website document (reference 29). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic search of case reports and pharmacovigilance reports for each opioid taken with an MAOI, with stated search terms and dates and each report assessed against the Hunter criteria by two readers; prospective data from people taking MAOIs who are given measured opioid exposures and examined for clonus and reflexes; and denominators for how many people took each pair, so that a rate can be stated.

domains.note: One sentence (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, about 40 reports) with no terms, dates or criteria; the case list is on the author’s website, outside the paper.

The 1968 test is appraised (reflexes and clonus not examined) and old reports are read against the modern definition, but individual fatality reports are not appraised, and the references given for fatalities include a rabbit study (reference 31) and a paper whose title concerns malignant hyperthermia with hypocalcaemia (reference 60), judged by their titles.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 12 of 84 references (18 to 29) are the author’s own; Tables 1 to 3 and the case list come from his own website document (reference 29); the spectrum concept and the reading of old reports rest on his 1998 review (reference 20).

Much is hedged (in my opinion, almost certainly, might possibly), but the abstract and conclusion state as known that the morphine-type drugs do not precipitate toxicity, on absence of reports, and that the 1968 test confirms the spectrum concept.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against serious reactions with opioids taken with MAOIs
domains.note: The null 1968 test and the uneventful uses of fentanyl are set against the case reports, and earlier reviews that called fentanyl safe are mentioned; but the argument that risk is probably low rests on reports the reader cannot see and gives no denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. The search is a single sentence, the case list is outside the paper, and a seventh of the references and the source of the tables are the author’s own. It may be cited for how one specialist reads the opioid and MAOI literature in 2005, for which opioids have and have not been reported with MAOIs in his judgment, and for what the 1968 test did and did not examine. It may not be cited for a rate of serious reactions, for any opioid being safe with an MAOI, or for the number or nature of the underlying fatalities.

key_findings.finding: The abstract states that serotonin toxicity is related to the concentration of serotonin at the synapse; that SRI overdoses frequently produce marked serotonergic side-effects and, in 15% of cases, moderate toxicity but not severe toxicity with hyperthermia and risk of death; that only combinations of serotonergic drugs acting by different mechanisms can raise serotonin to a life-threatening level; and that the combination that most commonly does so is an MAOI with any SRI, with lesser-known MAOIs (linezolid, moclobemide) and serotonergic opioids able to contribute.

The abstract states that the phenylpiperidine opioids pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan, and propoxyphene, appear to be weak serotonin reuptake inhibitors and have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities), and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be SRIs and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs.
key_findings.note: Table 2 says no reports are known for methadone; see the reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The Introduction says there have been periodic reviews of opioid analgesics in people taking MAOIs since 1955; that the difficulty has several causes: the reuptake-inhibiting capacity of opioids is only partly documented, there was until recently a lack of systematic data on the features of serotonin toxicity, and the spectrum concept, that it is dose-related and not idiosyncratic, is recent.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, right-hand column, paragraph beginning Ever since the initial report by Oates

key_findings.finding: Serotonin toxicity is described as a spectrum of serotonergic side-effects blending into toxicity, with a dose-effect relationship, and as a triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity (tremor, clonus, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, and in advanced stages pyramidal rigidity), autonomic hyperactivity (diaphoresis, fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea) and altered mental status (agitation, excitement, and in advanced stages confusion).
key_findings.locator: Definition and description (begins at the foot of p. 434, right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: The author summarises the Hunter decision rules from the Hunter Area Toxicology Service’s more than 2,000 prospectively documented overdose cases: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, allows serotonin toxicity to be reliably diagnosed. He says onset of frank toxicity is usually rapid because it follows drug combinations and starts when the second drug reaches effective blood levels, and that rigidity, a decreasing PaCO2 and a fever above 38.5 °C herald life-threatening toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Definition and description, paragraphs beginning The features that usually distinguish it and Clinically, the onset of frank toxicity (left-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia and anticholinergic delirium are said to be distinguishable from serotonin toxicity by onset (hours against days), by the presence of clonus and hyperreflexia and by dry skin and absent hyperreflexia in anticholinergic toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Definition and description, right-hand column (paragraphs beginning A possible differential diagnosis and NMS shares similarities)

key_findings.finding: Implicated drugs: the author states that the only therapeutic drugs implicated in severe reactions capable of precipitating fatalities are MAOIs with SRIs; that illicit stimulants such as MDMA, if combined with MAOIs (including moclobemide), also cause fatalities because they act as serotonin releasers; that serotonin releasers with MAOIs are the only other combination able to cause severe, potentially fatal toxicity; that several unpublished cases of MAOI and releaser combinations are known to him; and that a case series of four deaths has been reported by Vuori.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 435 and ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 436)

key_findings.finding: Theoretically a combination of amphetamine (but not methylphenidate) with an MAOI would precipitate serotonin toxicity, but the author says this is rarely encountered in practice and no fatalities are known.

Table 1 lists drugs with clinically relevant serotonergic potency (SRIs including tramadol, pethidine, fentanyl, methadone, dextromethorphan, dextropropoxyphene and pentazocine; the releasers amphetamine and MDMA; and the MAOIs including moclobemide and linezolid); its caption says fatalities from serotonin toxicity involving analgesics have been with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl.

Table 2 gives serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; lower is stronger) and reports with MAOIs: tramadol 760 and 528, definite, possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413 (weak, anomalous), definite, some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain, one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death; remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known but unlikely; morphine 500,000 and over 100,000, codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone over 100,000, none.
key_findings.note: The two Ki columns are other references and Codd; the table caption says the figures come from different sources and species and cannot be compared directly.

key_findings.finding: The author states a strong association between SRI potency and the ability to precipitate fatalities with MAOIs: affinities below 1 nM invariably go with the ability to precipitate toxicity and 1 to 10 nM is borderline; venlafaxine and tramadol are called anomalous because their estimated potency suggests they should not be a risk (possibly because they also release serotonin); pethidine is a very weak SRI whose discrepancy might be explained by releasing properties, with no direct evidence.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Overall, there is a strong association

key_findings.finding: The author says the early drugs involved in these interactions (pethidine and imipramine) are weak SRIs and, because there is a dose-effect relationship, usually fail to produce a reaction. He describes a 1968 test (Evans-Prosser) in which 15 patients were given injections of pethidine, morphine or water in graduated doses in hospital, in blind random order, to a maximum single pethidine dose of 75 mg and morphine 7.5 mg; none had serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus were not examined, only pulse and arterial pressure. He reads this as confirming that weak SRIs like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity, but only in susceptible people or with particularly large doses.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved (begins at the foot of the right-hand column of p. 436 and continues on p. 437)

key_findings.finding: In the same paragraph the author says about 40 reports of serotonin toxicity with analgesics, found by a search of the listed papers and standard databases, are listed on his website; that pethidine has undoubtedly caused a number of severe reactions and some fatalities and the other SRI analgesics have also precipitated some fatalities; that a small series at usual therapeutic doses may give a false sense of security because the dose-effect relationship is not appreciated; and that differences in cytochrome P450 enzymes produce 20 to 50-fold variations in serum levels between patients.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, same paragraph (sentences beginning The complete list of the references and Pethidine has undoubtedly caused)

key_findings.finding: The author says the limited clinical and experimental data agree that morphine analogues are not SRIs and none precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine), with no reports; that the phenylpiperidine opioids (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl and congeners, dextromethorphan, propoxyphene) are probably all borderline weak SRIs, and have been implicated in multiple reports almost certainly of serotonin toxicity, as judged by a subjective interpretation of the old case reports.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The limited available clinical and experimental data agree

key_findings.finding: In summary all the opioid analgesics with serotonergic effects have been involved in serotonin toxicity reports, but none of the drugs without SRI capacity have been; drugs with anomalous properties, like tramadol and pethidine, may yet be shown to act as serotonin releasers.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Details of all cases involving analgesics (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl: the author judges that one case report with a fatality (Noble) was probably serotonin toxicity, that another (Roy) may represent unrecognised toxicity, and that there is a question mark over fentanyl, although its potency as an SRI is low and it has been reported used with impunity; he thinks it probable that fentanyl has been used in many unreported cases with MAOIs because there was no problem, and says there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate of the risk, which would seem so low that one could not call its use strongly contra-indicated if there is no alternative. Remifentanil has no SRI data and its safe use with an MAOI has been reported.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning There are a few individual case reports worthy of particular comment (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Treatment section: an overdose of an SSRI alone produces at worst moderate toxicity (in 15% of cases enough for admission and active treatment) with no serious sequelae or fatalities; if an MAOI or a reversible MAOI plus an SRI were co-ingested in overdose, more than 50% of cases had severe toxicity (reference 38, not read); even therapeutic doses of moclobemide have been associated with severe toxicity when combined with SRIs, especially venlafaxine.
key_findings.locator: Treatment, 1st paragraph (beginning Careful consideration of the need for treatment)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are said to be known not to be SRIs and not to precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs; pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and methadone are said definitely to be weak SRIs that may infrequently precipitate dose-dependent toxicity with any type of MAOI, perhaps only in large doses or susceptible people. The author says the ability to estimate risk is compromised by a lack of systematically recorded clinical data and of precise potency data, and that for propoxyphene, pentazocine, fentanyl, remifentanil and congeners there are no SRI affinity data, so interpolation and the presence or absence of reports are used.

The author writes that the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low, but its unpredictable and serious nature makes it difficult to form judgments, and that any reaction is dose-dependent.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion, 2nd paragraph (beginning However, the clinical situation and the risks are now more clearly defined)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (p. 434), the discussion of the phenylpiperidine opioids (p. 437) and the conclusion (p. 439) place methadone among opioids that have been involved in, or may precipitate, serotonin toxicity with MAOIs; Table 2 says no reports are known for methadone, but unlikely.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not agree with itself on whether methadone has been reported with MAOIs; the table row, which is the more specific, says it has not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says pethidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and propoxyphene have all been involved in reactions with MAOIs including some fatalities; the Table 1 caption names fatalities only with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl; Table 2 lists fatalities only for pethidine (some) and tramadol (possible).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which opioids have been linked to deaths differs between the abstract and the tables; the tables are the more specific, and none of the three gives a number.

reporting_issues.issue: Borderline potency is defined as 1 to 10 nM, but the phenylpiperidine opioids are called probably all borderline although every value in Table 2 for them is above 10 nM (methadone 14.1 and 270, dextromethorphan 23, pethidine 413, tramadol 528 and 760).
reporting_issues.consequence: By the paper’s own bands these opioids are weaker than borderline, so the transporter data do not by themselves support the prediction that they can precipitate toxicity.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1968 test found no serotonergic symptoms in 15 patients at a maximum single pethidine dose of 75 mg, without examining reflexes or clonus, yet is described as confirming the spectrum concept, that weak SRIs like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity in susceptible people or with large doses.
reporting_issues.consequence: A null result that could not have detected the signs in question cannot show that the drug sometimes does precipitate toxicity; it shows only that no toxicity was recorded under those conditions.

reporting_issues.issue: The references given for fatalities with pethidine and the other SRI analgesics include a study in rabbits (reference 31) and a paper whose title concerns malignant hyperthermia associated with hypocalcaemia (reference 60), judged by their titles in the printed reference list; the cases are mostly from 1955 to 1971.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of human fatalities cannot be checked from the paper; some of the cited items may not be case reports of serotonin toxicity (the cited papers were not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The search is described in one sentence, and the list of about 40 reports, Tables 1 to 3 and the updated review are on the author’s website (reference 29), outside the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence behind each definite, possible or no reports entry is not in the paper and cannot be checked from it.

reporting_issues.issue: The Hunter rules are described as demonstrating clearly that serotonin toxicity may be reliably diagnosed on the stated findings, without the source paper’s caveats that its reference diagnosis was the same unit’s and that the rules need validating elsewhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Reliably is stronger than the source supports (see the card for Dunkley and colleagues, 2003).

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 434–441 (full text: abstract, introduction, Definition and description, Implicated drugs, Tables 1 and 2 (checked against a page render), Treatment, Conclusion, acknowledgements, reference list). The treatment doses and Table 3 were read for context only and are not recorded. The cited primary sources, the 1968 paper, the author’s website list and reference 38 were not read.
